{{Short description|Equivalence relation of groups}}
{{Use American English|date=January 2019}}
{{distinguish|Commensurability (mathematics)}}

In [[mathematics]], specifically in [[group theory]], two groups are '''commensurable''' if they differ only by a finite amount, in a precise sense. The '''commensurator''' of a [[subgroup]] is another subgroup, related to the [[normalizer]].

==Abstract commensurability==
Two [[group (mathematics)|group]]s ''G''<sub>1</sub> and ''G''<sub>2</sub> are said to be ('''abstractly''') '''commensurable''' if there are subgroups ''H''<sub>1</sub> ⊂ ''G''<sub>1</sub> and ''H''<sub>2</sub> ⊂ ''G''<sub>2</sub> of [[finite set|finite]] [[index (group theory)|index]] such that ''H''<sub>1</sub> is [[group isomorphism|isomorphic]] to ''H''<sub>2</sub>.<ref>Druțu & Kapovich (2018), Definition 5.13.</ref> For example:
*A group is finite if and only if it is commensurable with the trivial group.
*Any two finitely generated [[free group]]s on at least 2 generators are commensurable with each other.<ref>Druțu & Kapovich (2018), Proposition 7.80.</ref> The group [[modular group|''SL''(2,'''Z''')]] is also commensurable with these free groups.
*Any two [[surface group]]s of [[genus (mathematics)|genus]] at least 2 are commensurable with each other.

In [[geometric group theory]], a [[finitely generated group]] is viewed as a [[metric space]] using the [[word metric]]. If two groups are (abstractly) commensurable, then they are [[quasi-isometry|quasi-isometric]].<ref>Druțu & Kapovich (2018), Corollary 8.47.</ref> It has been fruitful to ask when the converse holds.

==Commensurability of subgroups==
A different but related notion is used for subgroups of a given group. Namely, two subgroups Γ<sub>1</sub> and Γ<sub>2</sub> of a group ''G'' are said to be '''commensurable''' if the [[intersection (set theory)|intersection]] Γ<sub>1</sub> ∩ Γ<sub>2</sub> is of finite index in both Γ<sub>1</sub> and Γ<sub>2</sub>. Clearly this implies that Γ<sub>1</sub> and Γ<sub>2</sub> are abstractly commensurable. 

Example: for nonzero [[real number]]s ''a'' and ''b'', the subgroup of '''R''' [[generating set of a group|generated]] by ''a'' is commensurable with the subgroup generated by ''b'' if and only if the real numbers ''a'' and ''b'' are [[commensurability (mathematics)|commensurable]], meaning that ''a''/''b'' belongs to the [[rational number]]s '''Q'''. If ''a'' and ''b'' are commensurable, with smallest positive common integer multiple ''c'', then <math>\langle a \rangle \cap \langle b \rangle = \langle c \rangle</math>, which has index ''c''/''|a|'' in <math>\langle a \rangle</math> and ''c''/''|b|'' in <math>\langle b \rangle</math>.

==Related notions==
{{main|Commensurability (mathematics)}}

===In linear algebra===
There is an analogous notion in linear algebra: two [[linear subspace]]s ''S'' and ''T'' of a [[vector space]] ''V'' are '''commensurable''' if the intersection ''S'' ∩ ''T'' has finite [[codimension]] in both ''S'' and ''T''.

===In topology===
Two [[path-connected]] [[topological space]]s are sometimes called ''commensurable'' if they have [[homeomorphism|homeomorphic]] finite-sheeted [[covering space]]s.  Depending on the type of space under consideration, one might want to use [[homotopy equivalence]]s or [[diffeomorphism]]s instead of homeomorphisms in the definition. By the relation between covering spaces and the [[fundamental group]], commensurable spaces have commensurable fundamental groups.

Example: the [[Gieseking manifold]] is commensurable with the complement of the [[figure-eight knot (mathematics)|figure-eight knot]]; these are both [[compact space|noncompact]] [[hyperbolic 3-manifold]]s of finite volume. On the other hand, there are infinitely many different commensurability classes of compact hyperbolic 3-manifolds, and also of noncompact hyperbolic 3-manifolds of finite volume.<ref>Maclachlan & Reid (2003), Corollary 8.4.2.</ref>

==Commensurators==
The '''commensurator''' of a subgroup Γ of a group ''G'', denoted Comm<sub>''G''</sub>(Γ), is the set of elements ''g'' of ''G'' that such that the [[inner automorphism|conjugate]] subgroup ''g''Γ''g''<sup>−1</sup> is commensurable with Γ.<ref>Druțu & Kapovich (2018), Definition 5.17.</ref>  In other words,
: <math>\operatorname{Comm}_G(\Gamma)=\{g\in G : g\Gamma g^{-1} \cap \Gamma \text{ has finite index in both } \Gamma \text{ and } g\Gamma g^{-1}\}.</math>
This is a subgroup of ''G'' that contains the [[normalizer]] N<sub>''G''</sub>(Γ) (and hence contains Γ).

For example, the commensurator of the [[special linear group]] ''SL''(''n'','''Z''') in ''SL''(''n'','''R''') contains ''SL''(''n'','''Q'''). In particular, the commensurator of ''SL''(''n'','''Z''') in ''SL''(''n'','''R''') is [[dense set|dense]] in ''SL''(''n'','''R'''). More generally, [[Grigory Margulis]] showed that the commensurator of a [[lattice (discrete subgroup)|lattice]] Γ in a [[semisimple Lie group]] ''G'' is dense in ''G'' if and only if Γ is an [[arithmetic subgroup]] of ''G''.<ref>Margulis (1991), Chapter IX, Theorem B.</ref>

==Abstract commensurators==

The '''abstract commensurator''' of a group <math>G</math>, denoted <math>\text{Comm}(G)</math>, is the group of equivalence classes of isomorphisms <math>\phi : H \to K</math>, where <math>H</math> and <math>K</math> are finite index subgroups of <math>G</math>, under composition.<ref>Druțu & Kapovich (2018), Section 5.2.</ref> Elements of <math>\text{Comm}(G)</math> are called '''commensurators''' of <math>G</math>.

If <math>G</math> is a connected [[Semisimple Lie group|semisimple]] [[Lie group]] not isomorphic to <math>\text{PSL}_2(\mathbb{R})</math>, with trivial center and no compact factors, then by the [[Mostow rigidity theorem]], the abstract commensurator of any irreducible [[lattice (group)|lattice]] <math>\Gamma \leq G</math> is linear. Moreover, if <math>\Gamma</math> is arithmetic, then Comm<math>(\Gamma)</math> is virtually isomorphic to a dense subgroup of <math>G</math>, otherwise Comm<math>(\Gamma)</math> is virtually isomorphic to <math>\Gamma</math>.
